messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

Bucket: negativas
Total de reviews analisadas neste bucket: 40

Reviews (nota em estrelas + texto completo):

[3] nota=0.5 estrelas:
The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Super sorry to everybody that loves this but no. I don't care how good the cinematography (10/10) and score (8 or 9/10) is, the finished product is in my opinion (and I can't stress the my opinion part enough) dogshit. The film has little to no talking and just has these two people doing chores for 154 FUCKING MINUTES. I like to get sucked into movies but I had to stop it halfway because this was too boring. It is extremely meditative, more so than "Tree of Life" but let me explain why I loved (and still adore) Tarr's Werckmeister Harmonies. It manages to have us get to know this young man through his attitude and mannerisms and his interactions with others. This film gave me nothing notable about these characters. It took stunning cinematography in the same location for so long that I begun to not care about the cinematography where Werckmeister changed locations all the time. That movie made me feel things. It was shocking, brutal, harrowing, and sad. I felt nothing watching this. That being said, the point of this is to show how mundane life was in the 18th century but you don't need a 154 minute film to do that. Read a history book (and I can't believe I'm saying this about a film so highly rated), it's much more enjoyable than this. 3/10 (unfortunately, pretty bad but it didn't hinder how much I adore Werckmeister. That movie pushed the line of my patience but never crossed. This movie crossed it not even an hour in. I do not reccomend to anyone that has precious free time and wants to enjoy it)

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

La película empieza poderosa, en medio de la tempestad, un hombre con su caballo intentando que el viento no se los lleve, una música ensordecedora y te meten una cita de Nietzsche en una transición igual de magnífica que el comienzo. Esos son los primeros cinco minutos de película, parecía pometedor y luego ves al hombre entrando en su rutina, se mete a casa y... empiezan a comer papas. Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. No pasa nada, no pasa más nada. Bien, me quieres vender la cotidianidad, pero, ¿me tenías que hacerme tragar la rutina de varios días del mismo hombre comiéndose unas papas? Más o menos a mitad de película llega un sujeto a la casa y dije: finalmente se dignaron a que pasara algo. Pero no, el sujeto era una herramienta al espectador para darnos contexto de toda la situación, pero la actuación es pobre y es una inmediata verborrea con toques líricos y poco destellos narrativos. Ahí dije: suficiente. No pude seguir viendo más, sé que pasa algo al final, pero no importa. Creo que estamos acostumbrados a que pase algo, sé que el director es así, la otra vez hizo tragarme 15 minutos de una persona caminando, pero la película duraba sus seis horas, quince minutos eran un pestañeo, pero aquí... esa grandilocuencia del inicio no se concreta con el hombre comiendo papas y menos con ese final que pareciera más el empate del inicio. Perfectamente la película se pudo haber terminado con el hombre comiendo papas y hubiese sido la misma basura. Decepcionante, aburrida y muy pobremente escrita. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.

4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".
